idiom_name: Promise.all over async tasks (I/O-bound); a node:worker_threads pool for CPU-bound parts
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no shared-memory threads on the main lane, so the classic master/worker structure is replaced by the event loop: for I/O-bound decomposition Promise.all (or allSettled) over async functions is the fan-out and its settlement is the aggregation - the master is the async function that awaits it, the workers are the promises. CPU-bound subtasks need real threads: node:worker_threads gives each Worker its own heap, tasks travel as structured-cloned messages (postMessage/parentPort) and the Node docs explicitly recommend a pool of Workers rather than one Worker per task; in browsers the equivalent is a Web Worker pool behind a message wrapper.
pitfalls: Promise.all rejects on the first failure while the remaining tasks keep running; use Promise.allSettled when every partial result (or failure) must be accounted for.
Threads do not share objects: worker messages are structured-cloned, so large payloads are copied - transfer ArrayBuffers or keep the payloads small.
A Worker keeps the event loop alive until terminate()/unref(), so an unclosed pool silently leaks threads and memory.
